title: Among People Who Hate Peace
sum: Psalm 120 is Psalm 119 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It opens the fifteen Songs of Ascents (120–134). A speaker who once cried to the LORD and was answered now cries again: lying tongues surround him, and he lives far from home among people who want war. The psalm ends with the trouble unresolved: "I am peace itself; but when I speak, / they are ready for war."

It is a strange way to begin a pilgrim songbook, and that may be the point. The journey "up" to Jerusalem starts from exile and hostility, among Meshech and Kedar, two far-off peoples. By Psalm 122 the pilgrim stands in Jerusalem's gates, and by 134 he is blessed in the temple at night.
readings: Read as a pilgrim's starting point
The speaker lives among foreigners or hostile neighbors and longs for the peace (shalom) of Jerusalem, which the next psalms reach (122:6–8). The collection moves from strife to the blessing of Zion.
Read as a prayer against slander

The speaker is falsely accused and prays for rescue from the lying tongue. The "arrows" and "coals" of 120:4 are either the tongue's own weapons or God's punishment on it. Rashi and the Targum read the psalm this way, of Doeg's lies against David or of Israel slandered among the nations.

views.H: The title names no author. Jewish tradition linked it to David fleeing Saul and slandered by Doeg (1 Samuel 22:9–10), or to Israel scattered among the nations.
views.C: Most scholars treat 120–134 as a collection of short songs, many from ordinary life (home, harvest, family), gathered for pilgrims after the exile (Crow; Seybold). Meshech (central Anatolia, far to the north) and Kedar (the north Arabian desert, to the south-east) are probably a figure of speech for living among barbarians, not two literal addresses.
views.L: Benedict's Rule assigns Psalms 120–128 to the short day hours of Terce, Sext and None on weekdays (Rule of Benedict 18), and the Roman Liturgy of the Hours uses the Songs of Ascents as the extra psalms for Daytime Prayer. The Orthodox Psalter reads 120–134 together as the eighteenth kathisma. In many Ashkenazi communities the fifteen songs are said on Sabbath afternoons in winter.
views.J: The Targum reads Meshech as "the Asians" and Kedar as "the Arabs," and makes 120:4 lightning from above and broom coals "that burn in Gehenna below." Rashi explains that broom coals look dead outside but stay alight inside, like slander, and the Talmud cites 120:3–4 on the punishment of slander (Bavli Arakhin 15b).
views.X: Augustine began his sermons on the Songs of Ascents here: the Christian climbs not with the feet but with the heart, and the climb starts from this world's "tents of Kedar" (Augustine, Expositions of the Psalms, on Psalm 119 in his numbering). Medieval Christians called 120–134 the Gradual Psalms (from Latin gradus, "step").

deep.b:
The fifteen titles say shir hamma'alot, "a song of the ascents" (121 has lamma'alot, "for the ascents"). Ma'alah means a step, a climb, or a going up.

1. Pilgrimage. Israelites "went up" to Jerusalem three times a year for the feasts (Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16), and Jerusalem stands high in the hills. Psalm 122:4 says "There the tribes went up." Isaiah speaks of singing "as when one goes with the flute to come to the mountain of the LORD" (Isaiah 30:29, fresh rendering), and the Mishnah describes villagers going up with their firstfruits, called to "rise, and let us go up to Zion" (Mishnah Bikkurim 3:2, quoting Jeremiah 31:6). Most scholars hold this view.

2. The temple steps. The Mishnah says fifteen steps led from the Court of the Women up to the Court of Israel, "corresponding to the fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms," and that on the Feast of Booths the Levites stood on them with lyres, harps and trumpets and sang (Mishnah Middot 2:5; Mishnah Sukkah 5:4). The Mishnah does not say they sang these psalms there, only that the number matches. The Greek ōdē tōn anabathmōn and the Latin canticum graduum both mean "song of the steps."

3. The return from exile. Ezra 7:9 calls the return "the journey up from Babylon" (hamma'alah), and several songs speak of restored fortunes (126) and of Israel's long trouble (129). Some scholars, Goulder among them, link the collection to Nehemiah's time.

4. A style of "stepping" verse. Many of these psalms repeat a word from one line to start the next (121:3–4 "doze"; 121:7–8 "guard"; 124:3–5 "then"). Gesenius and others suggested the name comes from this stair-step parallelism. Few hold it as the whole explanation, but the style is real.

The views can overlap: songs sung on the way up could be gathered after the return and later linked with the temple steps.

The base text is the Leningrad Codex (texts/orig). For the Greek, Codex Vaticanus is lost for these psalms, so Swete's edition prints Codex Sinaiticus, with the readings of Alexandrinus and of the Verona and Zurich Psalters in its apparatus; readings found in only one of these are named by their manuscript, and the standard critical text (Rahlfs) is cited where it is reported to differ. The writer checked personally: Swete's Greek text and apparatus; both of Jerome's Latin Psalters (the Gallican and the Psalter from the Hebrew); the Qumran Hebrew of 11QPs-a, 11QPs-b, 1QPs-b, 4QPs-e, 4QPs-k and 4QPs-n in the ETCBC transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook; the Targum; Rashi; Midrash Tehillim (in a loose English version); and the Mishnah and Talmud passages cited. The Syriac Peshitta was not consulted; where it is mentioned (137:8), it is reported from the BHS apparatus.

deep.h: How the fifteen songs are arranged
deep.b:
The collection seems to be built with care. Psalm 127, the only one linked to Solomon, stands in the middle with seven songs on either side. Four name David (122, 124, 131, 133). The name YHWH occurs often and the short form Yah only twice (122:4; 130:3). The songs move from a far land (120) to Jerusalem's gates (122), through trouble and rescue (123–129), to forgiveness (130), humility (131), the ark and David's house (132), unity (133), and finally the night blessing in the temple (134). The collection is a unit in the Hebrew Psalter but not everywhere: in the Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPs-a), Psalms 121–132 stand together in order, but 119 follows 132, then 135 and 136, while 133, 134 and 137 appear elsewhere in the scroll (Flint; Abegg, Flint and Ulrich). Repeated phrases bind them: "maker of heaven and earth" (121:2; 124:8; 134:3), "from this moment on and for all time" (121:8; 125:2; 131:3), "Peace on Israel!" (125:5; 128:6), "let Israel say" (124:1; 129:1).

The Talmud tells a legend about the number: when David dug the temple's foundations, the waters of the deep rose to flood the world, and David sang fifteen Songs of Ascents to make them go down (Bavli Sukkah 53a). Some Christian writers linked the fifteen to the fifteen years added to Hezekiah's life (Isaiah 38:5), when the shadow went back on the "steps" (ma'alot) of Ahaz (Isaiah 38:8).

echoes: Psalm 122:4; Psalm 134:3; Ezra 7:9; Isaiah 30:29; Isaiah 38:8; Genesis 10:2; Genesis 25:13; Jeremiah 2:10; Jeremiah 9:3–8; James 3:5–8; Romans 12:18; Hebrews 12:14

settings.what: A cry against lying tongues, from a speaker living far from home
settings.by: an Israelite who lives among hostile foreigners or slanderers (120:5–7)
settings.to: the LORD (120:1–2), the lying tongue itself (120:3–4), and the speaker's own heart (120:5–7)
settings.when: the title: one of the Songs of Ascents; scholars suggest a pilgrim from the dispersion, or an Israelite at home surrounded by hostile neighbors
settings.why: to bring false accusation before God and to name the longing for peace that the pilgrimage to Jerusalem will answer
settings.readers: Jews scattered in the Persian and later empires, living "in Meshech" and "Kedar," sang it as the first step home.
views: A Jew living in the dispersion sets out for Jerusalem (Crow, Hossfeld and Zenger).
"Meshech" and "Kedar" are figures for hostile neighbors (Allen, Goldingay).
Jewish tradition: David slandered before Saul (Rashi).

title: The Guard Who Never Sleeps
sum: Psalm 121 is Psalm 120 in the Greek and Latin numbering. A traveler looks toward the hills and asks where help will come from. The answer is the LORD, "maker of heaven and earth." Then another voice, perhaps a priest, a parent or the traveler's own heart, promises that the LORD will guard him: he never dozes, he is shade at the right hand, and he will guard every going out and coming in.

The Hebrew word shamar, "guard, keep," comes six times in eight verses. It is one of the best-loved psalms in Judaism and Christianity, said before journeys, at the bedside of the sick, and at funerals.
readings: Read as a pilgrim's blessing

Pilgrims setting out for Jerusalem, or leaving it, exchange words: one asks where help comes from (121:1–2), another answers with a blessing (121:3–8). The hills are the hills of the road, with their dangers.
Read as a statement of faith against other gods
The hills were the site of shrines to other gods. "Where does my help come from?" means "not from the high places": help comes only from the maker of heaven and earth (compare Jeremiah 3:23).

views.H: The title names no author. Jewish readers have heard the voice of Israel in exile, or of Jacob setting out from home (Genesis 28), to whom God promised, "Look, I am with you. I will guard you everywhere you go" (Genesis 28:15).
views.C: Scholars debate whether the psalm is a dialogue, a liturgy of blessing at the temple gate, or a single speaker who addresses himself. The change from "my help" (121:1–2) to "your foot" (121:3) suggests two voices. The language of a god who "does not sleep" may answer the idea of gods who sleep (1 Kings 18:27).
views.L: Christians and Jews use it as a travelers' psalm; in the Orthodox and Anglican traditions it is often read before journeys, and many churches use it at funerals and gravesides. The Scottish metrical version "I to the hills will lift mine eyes" is sung widely. Mendelssohn set 121:4 in Elijah as "He, watching over Israel, slumbers not, nor sleeps."
views.J: In many Jewish homes Psalm 121 is printed on amulets and cards hung in the room of a mother in childbirth and her newborn. It is also part of the prayer for travelers and is recited at the graveside. The Targum says the LORD casts shade on you "on account of the mezuzah" fixed to the right side of your door (121:5) and, like every Song of Ascents, heads it as a song "said on the ascents from the abyss" (see the chapter page of Psalm 120).
views.X: Christians have read "the LORD will guard your going out and your coming in" of the whole of life, from birth to death. Augustine heard the hills as the apostles and prophets through whom God's help comes, while the help itself comes only from God.

deep.b:
The verb shamar, "guard, keep," carries the psalm: "the one who guards you" (121:3), "the one who guards Israel" (121:4), "your guardian" (121:5), "will guard you ... will guard your very life" (121:7), "will guard your going out" (121:8). The word is used of shepherds keeping sheep (Genesis 30:31), watchmen keeping a city (127:1), and the priestly blessing: "May the LORD bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24). The stair-step style of the Songs of Ascents is clear here: "doze" in 121:3 is picked up in 121:4, and "guard" in 121:7 in 121:8.

The dangers are those of the road: a slip on rocky paths, sunstroke, the night. "The moon" striking by night may reflect an old belief that moonlight caused illness (the English word "lunatic" comes from it; compare Matthew 4:24 and 17:15, where the Greek speaks of being "moon-struck"). The psalm answers every fear with the same promise.

echoes: Genesis 28:15; Genesis 28:20–22; Numbers 6:24; Isaiah 27:3; Isaiah 49:10; 1 Kings 18:27; Jeremiah 3:23; John 17:12; Revelation 7:16; 2 Thessalonians 3:3

settings.what: A question and an answer of blessing for a traveler
settings.by: a traveler (121:1–2), and a second voice that blesses him (121:3–8), or one speaker addressing himself
settings.to: first the speaker's own heart, then the traveler as "you"
settings.when: the title: a Song for the Ascents; many scholars think of pilgrims leaving home or leaving Jerusalem, perhaps blessed by a priest
settings.why: to send a traveler out with assurance that the Creator himself guards the road, by day and by night
settings.readers: Jews scattered across the Persian empire used it as a blessing for the long journey to Jerusalem and home again.
views: Pilgrims blessed as they leave Jerusalem (Hossfeld and Zenger, Allen).
A traveler sets out toward the hills of Judah (Kraus).
The speaker answers his own question (Goldingay, Alter).

title: Standing in Jerusalem's Gates
sum: Psalm 122 is Psalm 121 in the Greek and Latin numbering. A pilgrim remembers the joy of the invitation, "Let's go to the LORD's house," and now stands in Jerusalem's gates. He praises the city, built close and joined as one, where the tribes go up and where David's house sits in judgment. Then he prays for its peace, for the sake of his brothers and friends and of the LORD's house.

The psalm plays on the city's name: Yerushalayim sounds like shalom, "peace," and shalvah, "ease" (122:6–7). It is the psalm of the pilgrim's arrival, and the source of the phrase "pray for the peace of Jerusalem."
readings: Read as the arrival of pilgrims
The pilgrims have arrived ("Our feet were standing") and look back to the day they set out ("I was full of joy when they told me"). Jerusalem is the center of worship and of justice.
Read as a song of David's city
The title names David, and the psalm praises "thrones that belong to David's house" (122:5). The Talmud and Rashi read it as David's prophecy of the temple that his son would build.

views.H: The title says "Of David." Some Greek copies leave it out (see the variant). Since the temple ("the LORD's house") was built after David, Jewish tradition read the psalm as David's foresight; others take "of David" as "for David's house" or "in David's manner."
views.C: Most scholars date it to the time of the temple, before or after the exile, as a pilgrim song. "Thrones for judging" (122:5) may recall that the king's court sat in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 15:2–4; 1 Kings 7:7), or after the exile, the hope of David's house.
views.L: Psalm 122 is a common entrance psalm. Hubert Parry's anthem "I was glad" (1902), written for the coronation of Edward VII, has been sung at every British coronation since; Purcell and others set it before him. Catholics use it at Evening Prayer and on feasts of the dedication of a church. It is often sung as pilgrims enter Jerusalem.
views.J: "Our feet were standing in your gates" was read by the Talmud of the courts of law: what kept Israel's feet firm in war was the courts of Jerusalem where Torah was studied (Bavli Makkot 10a). The Targum reads "joined into one" (122:3) of the Jerusalem "built in the firmament" joined to the city on earth, an idea also in the Talmud (Bavli Taanit 5a).
views.X: Christians have read the psalm of the church and of the heavenly Jerusalem (Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2). Augustine said its people "go up" by love. Many Christians today pray 122:6 for the city of Jerusalem and its people, Jewish, Christian and Muslim alike.

deep.h: "Ask for peace for Jerusalem": a play on the name
deep.b:
Verses 6–8 are full of sounds that echo the city's name. Sha'alu shelom Yerushalayim, "ask for the peace of Jerusalem"; yishlayu, "may they be at ease"; shalom, "peace"; shalvah, "quiet"; and again shalom in 122:8. The ancient name Urusalim appears in the Amarna letters (1300s BC), and its meaning is debated, perhaps "foundation of (the god) Shalem." Israel heard shalom in it.

"Peace" here is more than the absence of war: it is welfare, wholeness, and right order. The prayer is for the city's walls ("ramparts") and strongholds, for its people ("those who love you"), and for its center, "the house of the LORD our God" (122:9). Jeremiah told the exiles to "seek the peace of the city" of Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7, fresh rendering). Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it had not recognized "what leads to peace" (Luke 19:42).

echoes: Isaiah 2:3; Micah 4:2; Deuteronomy 16:16; 2 Samuel 15:2–4; Jeremiah 29:7; Luke 2:41–42; Luke 19:41–42; Galatians 4:26; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2

settings.what: A pilgrim's arrival in Jerusalem and a prayer for its peace
settings.by: a pilgrim ("I") speaking for a group ("our feet"); the title names David
settings.to: the speaker's companions, then Jerusalem itself (122:2, 6–9)
settings.when: the title: a Song of Ascents of David; most scholars place it at the end of a pilgrimage to one of the three feasts, in the time of the temple
settings.why: to celebrate the city as the center of Israel's worship and justice and to pray for its peace
settings.readers: Jews after the exile, whose city was poor and whose king was gone, sang of the tribes going up and of David's thrones as a hope still to be fulfilled.
views: Spoken on arrival at the feast (Allen, Kraus).
Spoken as the pilgrims leave, looking back (Crow).
David foresees the temple (Rashi, the Talmud).

title: Eyes on the Master's Hand
sum: Psalm 123 is Psalm 122 in the Greek and Latin numbering. In four verses the speaker lifts his eyes to God in heaven and compares the people to slaves who watch their master's hand, waiting for him to show favor. Then comes the plea: "Be gracious to us, LORD, be gracious to us!" They have had their fill of the contempt of the comfortable and the proud.
The psalm is a short communal lament. It names no enemy and no event, only the long weariness of being despised. Its picture of eyes fixed on a hand has made it a psalm of patient waiting.
readings: Read as patient waiting
The slaves' eyes on the master's hand show attention and readiness: they wait for a sign, a command, or a gift. Israel waits for God "until he is gracious to us," trusting but not demanding.
Read as a plea against oppressors
The slaves look to the hand that can strike or spare. The psalm is a cry from a people under foreign rule, mocked by those at ease (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:1–4), asking God to end it.

views.H: The title gives no author. The Midrash on Psalms applies it to Israel in every exile.
views.C: Scholars date it after the exile, comparing the contempt the returned community faced from Sanballat and others (Nehemiah 2:19; 4:1–4). The move from "I" (123:1) to "we" (123:2–4) suggests a leader praying for the people.
views.L: The Liturgy of the Hours uses it at Evening Prayer on Monday of week three. In the Roman Gradual its first verse, Ad te levavi oculos meos, is the Tract of the Third Sunday of Lent.
views.J: Rashi notes the word "you whose seat is in the heavens": God is enthroned above, while Israel waits below. The Ketiv and Qere in 123:4 differ (see the variant); later Jewish readers heard "the proud of the Greeks" in the marginal reading.
views.X: Christians have read the servant's watchful eyes as a picture of prayer and obedience (Luke 12:35–38). The Rule of Benedict's call to listen "with the ear of the heart" has often been linked with such texts.

deep.b:
The comparison would have been plain in the ancient world, where household slaves were common. A slave watched for the master's hand to signal what to do, to give food or wages, or to grant a request. The psalm uses both a man ("their master's hand") and a woman ("her mistress's hand"), as if to include everyone in the household. The plural "masters" (adonim) may be a plural of rank, as often for God.

The psalm does not approve of slavery; it uses a picture its hearers knew. Its point is dependence: "until he is gracious to us." The same posture of waiting is found in 25:15, "My eyes are always on the LORD" and in the waiting of 130:5–6.

echoes: Psalm 25:15; Psalm 121:1; Nehemiah 2:19; Nehemiah 4:1–4; Isaiah 37:16–17; Luke 12:35–38; Psalm 44:13–16

settings.what: A people's plea for mercy under contempt
settings.by: a leader ("I") who speaks for the people ("we")
settings.when: no event is named; scholars suggest the hard years after the return from exile
settings.why: to put the community's humiliation before God and to wait on him with trust
settings.readers: Israel in the Persian period and under later empires, mocked and powerless, sang it as the prayer of a people still waiting.
views: The community despised by its neighbors (Allen, Hossfeld and Zenger).

title: If the LORD Had Not Been With Us
sum: Psalm 124 is Psalm 123 in the Greek and Latin numbering. A leader calls on Israel to say it together: if the LORD had not been on our side, our enemies would have swallowed us alive, the flood would have closed over our heads. Instead, like a bird from a broken trap, "we got loose." The psalm ends with a confession: "Our help is in the name of the LORD, / maker of heaven and earth."
It is a communal thanksgiving with the stair-step style of the Songs of Ascents: "then ... then ... then" (124:3–5), "we got loose ... the trap snapped ... we got loose" (124:7).
readings: Read as thanks for a past rescue
Israel looks back on a real danger that nearly destroyed it, from the exodus to the return. The images of flood and trap describe how close it came.
Read as a liturgy for every rescue
The psalm is a call and response for worship. Its last verse became a standard opening for prayer, so that every gathering begins by confessing that help comes from the Creator alone.

views.H: The title says "Of David." The Targum calls it a song "said on the ascents from the abyss, by David."
views.C: Many scholars note Aramaic-like forms (she- for "who"; 'azay, "then") and date it after the exile. The "waters, swollen with pride" (124:5) use the old image of chaos waters (69:1–2; Isaiah 8:7–8).
views.L: Calvin's Geneva church began its Sunday service with 124:8, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth," and Reformed churches still use it as the opening words of worship (Calvin's form of prayers, 1542). The Latin form Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini opens Compline and many blessings in the Western church.
views.J: The Midrash and Rashi apply it to the Exodus, to Haman, and to every later persecution.
views.X: Huguenots sang the Genevan setting of Psalm 124 (the "Old 124th") in times of persecution. It was sung in Geneva after the failed Savoyard attack on the city in 1602 (the Escalade). Christians hear in 124:7 the church's escape from the snares of the devil (2 Timothy 2:26).

deep.h: "Our help is in the name of the LORD"
deep.b:
The last verse has had a long life apart from the psalm. In the Latin West, Adiutorium nostrum in nomine Domini / Qui fecit caelum et terram opens Compline and many rites of blessing. John Calvin made it the opening of the Lord's Day service in Geneva (La forme des prières, 1542), and Reformed and Presbyterian churches still begin worship with it, called the "votum." The phrase "maker of heaven and earth" links the Songs of Ascents (121:2; 134:3) and passed into the Apostles' Creed.

The "name" of the LORD stands for his presence and character, the God who made himself known (Exodus 3:15; Exodus 34:5–7). Help is not in a charm or a formula but in the one who is named.

echoes: Psalm 121:2; Psalm 134:3; Psalm 69:1–2; Psalm 91:3; Exodus 15:8–10; Isaiah 8:7–8; Isaiah 43:2; Romans 8:31; 2 Timothy 2:26

settings.what: A thanksgiving for national rescue, in call and response
settings.by: a leader (124:1, "let Israel say") and the people
settings.to: the congregation throughout; 124:6 blesses the LORD in the third person
settings.when: the title: of David; no event is named; scholars suggest a festival after a deliverance, or the return from exile
settings.why: to teach the people to say together that their survival is God's doing
settings.readers: Israel after the exile, small among the nations, confessed its survival as a gift and its help in the Creator's name.
views: Late language and theme of survival (Allen, Hossfeld and Zenger).
Following the title, a deliverance in the time of the kings (Dahood).

title: Like the Mountains Around Jerusalem
sum: Psalm 125 is Psalm 124 in the Greek and Latin numbering. Those who trust the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, and the LORD surrounds his people as the mountains surround Jerusalem. The rule of the wicked will not last on the land of the righteous, lest they too turn to evil. The psalm ends with a prayer, "LORD, be good to the good," a warning for those who turn aside, and a blessing: "Peace on Israel!"
It is a psalm of trust for a people under foreign rule. Its image comes straight from Jerusalem's geography: the city sits on a ridge surrounded by higher hills.
readings: Read as trust under foreign rule
"The rod of the wicked" is foreign rule over the land of Israel (125:3). The psalm promises it will not last forever, and warns that long oppression tempts even the righteous to compromise.
Read as wisdom about two ways
The psalm contrasts the good and the crooked, like Psalm 1. God's protection is for those "straight in heart"; those who "bend off onto their twisting paths" share the fate of evildoers.

views.H: The title names no author. Rashi applies it to Israel in exile, trusting in God.
views.C: Scholars date it to the Persian or early Greek period, when foreign governors ruled the land (Nehemiah 5:15). "The share of land ... drew by lot" (125:3) recalls the division of Canaan by lot (Joshua 14:2).
views.L: The Liturgy of the Hours uses it at Daytime Prayer. Its closing words "Peace on Israel!" (also 128:6) were carved on synagogue mosaics, as at the ancient synagogue at Jericho (about the 500s AD), which reads shalom 'al Yisra'el.
views.J: Rashi reads 125:2 with sorrow: though mountains surround Jerusalem, she is weak and nations rule her, until God's people are within her and he surrounds them. Rashi and the Targum read 125:3 as a promise that God will not let the rule of the wicked rest on the righteous.
views.X: Christians read 125:1 of the believer's security in God (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:38–39).

deep.b:
Verse 3 is the center: "The rod of the wicked will not stay / on the share of land the righteous drew by lot." The "rod" (shevet) is a scepter, the sign of rule. The land was given to Israel's tribes by lot as an inheritance (Joshua 14:2; Numbers 26:55); foreign rule over it seemed to break God's gift.

The psalm gives a striking reason why the oppression must end: "Otherwise the righteous might reach out / and turn their hands to wrong." Long injustice can wear down good people until they give up and join the wrongdoers. The psalm trusts God to set a limit (compare 1 Corinthians 10:13).

echoes: Psalm 46:5; Psalm 48:1–3; Psalm 1:1–6; Psalm 128:6; Zechariah 2:5; Joshua 14:2; Isaiah 54:10; 1 Corinthians 10:13; Galatians 6:16

settings.what: A song of trust and a blessing on Israel
settings.by: a leader or priest speaking to and for the congregation
settings.to: the congregation (125:1–3), then the LORD (125:4), then a blessing on Israel (125:5)
settings.when: no event is named; scholars suggest foreign rule over the land in the Persian or Greek period
settings.why: to strengthen trust in a time of foreign domination and to warn against giving in to it
settings.readers: Israel under the Persian and Greek empires, governed by outsiders, held to the promise that the land and the people were still the LORD's.
views: Under foreign governors after the return (Allen).
Under Ptolemies or Seleucids (some older critics).

title: Sowing in Tears
sum: Psalm 126 is Psalm 125 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It remembers a day when the LORD turned Zion's fortunes back and the people were "like people dreaming," laughing and shouting, while the nations said, "The LORD has done something great with them." Then it prays for the same again: "LORD, turn our fortunes back again, / like the stream beds in the Negev." It ends with a farmer's promise: those who sow in tears will reap with joy.
The psalm holds together joy already tasted and joy still hoped for. Most readers link it to the return from exile and the hard years after.
readings: Read as past joy and present prayer
Verses 1–3 recall the return from Babylon (538 BC); verses 4–6 pray for full restoration in a time of drought and poverty (Haggai 1:6–11). The pattern is "you did it once; do it again."
Read as future hope

The verbs of 126:1–3 can be taken as future, as in many Jewish prayers: "When the LORD restores Zion, we will be like dreamers." The psalm then looks to the final redemption, and the sowing in tears is the long exile.

views.H: The title names no author. Jewish tradition read it of the return from Babylon and of the future redemption.
views.C: Scholars debate the tenses: the perfect verbs in 126:1–3 can be past or prophetic. The image of the Negev wadis and the farmer's year suggests a time of drought. A link to an ancient Near Eastern ritual of weeping at sowing has been proposed but is doubtful (see the note on 126:5).
views.L: Jews sing Psalm 126 before the grace after meals on Sabbaths and festivals, often to joyful tunes. Christians use it at Evening Prayer and at harvest services; Brahms set 126:5–6 in the first movement of A German Requiem (1868) as words of comfort for mourners.
views.J: The Talmud tells of Honi the circle-drawer, who could not understand how seventy years of exile could seem "like a dream," and slept for seventy years himself (Bavli Taanit 23a). Rashi reads the tears as acts of charity sown in exile, to be reaped at the redemption.
views.X: Christians have read the sowing in tears of Christ's death and the harvest of his resurrection (John 12:24; John 16:20), and of all Christian work done in hope (Galatians 6:9). The hymn "Bringing in the Sheaves" (1874) takes its words from 126:6.

deep.b:
The return from Babylon seemed too good to be true. Cyrus's decree in 538 BC (Ezra 1:1–4) let the exiles go home and rebuild the temple, and the prophets had promised a return with singing (Isaiah 35:10; 51:11; Jeremiah 31:12). The psalm says the nations noticed: "The LORD has done something great with them" (126:2). Israel echoes them: "The LORD has done something great with us" (126:3).

Yet the next verse prays for restoration again. The returned community was small, poor and often hungry (Haggai 1:6; Nehemiah 5:1–5). The Negev's dry wadis that fill in a single storm picture the hope: not a slow recovery but a sudden flood of grace. The last two verses turn the hope into a law of the farmer's year: seed is sown with weeping, because it may be the last grain the family has, yet the harvest comes "with a ringing shout." The doubled verbs ("He goes and goes ... he will come, yes, come") make the long walk of the sower and the sure return of the reaper.

echoes: Ezra 1:1–4; Isaiah 35:10; Isaiah 51:11; Jeremiah 31:9–13; Joel 2:21; Haggai 1:6–11; Luke 6:21; John 16:20–22; Galatians 6:9; 2 Corinthians 9:6

settings.what: Remembered joy and a prayer for restoration
settings.to: the LORD (126:4), and the community itself (126:1–3, 5–6)
settings.when: no event is named; most scholars think of the return from Babylon and the hard years that followed
settings.why: to keep alive the memory of God's great deed and to pray for its completion, in the hope of the harvest
settings.readers: Jews after the return, and in every later exile, sang it as both memory and hope.
views: The whole psalm looks to the coming restoration (some Jewish readers, Dahood).
A song for the autumn feast after drought (Mowinckel).

title: If the LORD Does Not Build
sum: Psalm 127 is Psalm 126 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It is a wisdom psalm in two parts. The first says that work without the LORD is "for nothing": building, guarding, rising early and staying up late. The LORD gives rest to the one he loves. The second calls children, especially sons, an inheritance from the LORD, like arrows in a fighter's hand, so that a father with many will not be put to shame at the gate.

It stands at the center of the fifteen Songs of Ascents and is the only one linked to Solomon. The Latin Nisi Dominus has been a motto for cities, universities and builders, and the psalm is sung at weddings and house blessings.
readings: Read as wisdom about work
The psalm warns against anxious overwork, not against work. Effort that forgets God is "for nothing"; rest is his gift. Children too are his gift, not a human achievement.
Read as a song of David's house and the temple
The "house" is the temple Solomon built and the dynasty God built for David (2 Samuel 7:11–13). Solomon, called Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD" (2 Samuel 12:25), is "the one he loves" (127:2).

views.H: The title says "Of Solomon." Rashi says David spoke it about Solomon, who would build the temple. The Greek text in Swete's edition has no name in the title (see the variant).
views.C: Most scholars see two proverbs joined, like Proverbs 10:22 ("It is the LORD's blessing that makes a person rich, / and toil adds nothing to it"). The link to Solomon may come from the word "house" and from yedido, "his beloved."
views.L: "Nisi Dominus" is the motto of the city of Edinburgh in shortened form and of many colleges. Monteverdi set it in his Vespers of 1610, and Vivaldi and Handel wrote settings. It is used in the Catholic and Anglican rites for blessing a home, and at weddings.
views.J: Rashi applies "sons" to disciples a teacher raises, and "enemies in the gate" to scholars who argue over Torah as if enemies and remain friends (Bavli Kiddushin 30b). The Talmud also reads 127:2 as a word about Torah study late at night.
views.X: Christians have read "the house" of the church built by Christ (Matthew 16:18; 1 Corinthians 3:9–11) and of the home. The psalm stands behind debates over family size and birth control; see the box below.

deep.b:
The word shav', "emptiness, in vain," comes three times in two verses: builders work for nothing, the watchman stays awake for nothing, you rise early for nothing. It is the word of the third commandment, "You must not take up the name of the LORD your God for something empty" (Exodus 20:7), and of empty idols (31:6). The psalm does not condemn building, guarding or rising early. It says these alone, without the LORD, cannot secure a house, a city or a life. The picture of eating "bread earned with pain" (127:2) recalls the curse on Adam (Genesis 3:17); trust in God's gift breaks the curse's grip.

The turn to children (127:3–5) follows naturally: in Hebrew a "house" is a household, and sons (banim) are what "builds" (banah) it. Ruth 4:11 blesses Ruth to be like Rachel and Leah, "who built the house of Israel."

echoes: Genesis 3:17–19; Genesis 33:5; Ruth 4:11; 2 Samuel 7:11–13; 2 Samuel 12:24–25; Proverbs 10:22; Ecclesiastes 2:22–24; Matthew 6:25–34; Mark 4:26–29; 1 Corinthians 3:6–11

settings.what: Two wisdom sayings on work and children
settings.by: a wisdom teacher; the title names Solomon
settings.to: the listener ("you," 127:2), and anyone building a house or a family
settings.when: the title: a Song of Ascents of Solomon; scholars see a proverb used by pilgrims, perhaps at the center of the collection
settings.why: to teach that every human effort, from building to raising children, depends on God's gift
settings.readers: Jewish families after the exile, rebuilding homes and city walls (Nehemiah 4), heard that their labor and their children were both God's work.
views: A wisdom saying on work and one on children (Allen, Kraus).
Solomon's house and David's line (Rashi, some modern readers).
Linked to Nehemiah's building and guarding (Goulder).

traditions.q: Does "Happy is the man who has filled his quiver" rule out birth control?
views: Children are "the supreme gift of marriage" (Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes 50; Catechism 2378). Each act of marriage must stay open to life, so artificial contraception is excluded, while couples may space births for serious reasons using natural periods of infertility (Paul VI, Humanae Vitae 10–16, 1968; Catechism 2366–2370).

The Russian Orthodox Church's 2000 social teaching rejects abortifacients but does not equate other contraception with abortion, leaving married couples to decide with their spiritual father; the ideal remains openness to children.

The Lambeth Conference of 1930 (Resolution 15) first allowed contraception where there is "a clearly felt moral obligation to limit or avoid parenthood," and most Anglican churches now leave family planning to the couple's conscience.

Most evangelicals accept non-abortive birth control as a matter of conscience. A minority, often called the Quiverfull movement (Mary Pride, The Way Home, 1985), reads 127:3–5 as a call to receive as many children as God sends without contraception.

title: The Table of One Who Fears the LORD
sum: Psalm 128 is Psalm 127 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It blesses everyone who fears the LORD: they will eat what their hands have worked for; the wife will be like a fruitful vine in the inner rooms, the children like young olive plants around the table. Then a priestly blessing reaches from Zion to the home: may you see Jerusalem's good all your life, and your children's children. "Peace on Israel!"

It is the companion of Psalm 127: there work and children were God's gift; here they are his blessing on those who fear him. The picture moves outward from the family table to the city and the nation.
readings: Read as a blessing on the household
A priest or elder blesses a pilgrim and his family. The fear of the LORD brings a full table, a fruitful home, and long life, as wisdom promises (Proverbs 3:1–10).
Read as the blessing of the covenant
The psalm turns the covenant curses around: others will not eat your harvest (Deuteronomy 28:30–33), and your children will live in peace in the land. The home's welfare is tied to Jerusalem's.

views.H: The title names no author. Rashi reads it of those who live by their own work, and notes that "each one" includes women.
views.C: Scholars call it a wisdom psalm with a priestly blessing (128:5–6). It may have been spoken as pilgrims returned home from Jerusalem, or at a wedding.
views.L: Psalm 128 is one of the psalms most often used at Christian weddings, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant. The Roman rite of marriage offers it as the responsorial psalm, and the Orthodox wedding service sings it as the couple is led in procession. It is also sung at Jewish weddings in some communities.
views.J: The Talmud quotes 128:2, "Happy are you ... it will go well for you," of a person who earns his own living: "happy" in this world and "well" in the world to come (Bavli Berakhot 8a). It is said on Saturday evening at the close of the Sabbath in many homes.
views.X: Christians have read the vine and the olive plants of Christ and his church (John 15:1–5; Romans 11:17–24), and of the Christian home as a small church.

deep.h: From the table to the nation
deep.b:
The blessing widens in circles. It begins with "each one who fears the LORD" (128:1), moves to his work (128:2), to his wife and children at the table (128:3), back to the man (128:4), then to Zion and Jerusalem (128:5), to grandchildren, and finally to all Israel (128:6). The family's welfare depends on the city's, and the city's on God's blessing from Zion. The same order is found in Jeremiah's letter: "seek the welfare of the city ... for in its welfare you will have welfare" (Jeremiah 29:7, fresh rendering).

The images are of an Israelite farm: the vine and the olive, the two great crops of the hills (Micah 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:8). The wife "deep inside the house" is not hidden but at the center of the home, where its life is.

echoes: Deuteronomy 8:8; Deuteronomy 28:4; Deuteronomy 28:30–33; Proverbs 3:1–10; Proverbs 31:10–31; Micah 4:4; Isaiah 65:21–23; Numbers 6:24–26; Psalm 127:3–5; John 15:1–5

settings.what: A blessing on the household of one who fears the LORD
settings.to: the one who fears the LORD ("you")
settings.when: no occasion is named; scholars suggest pilgrims blessed before returning home, or a wedding
settings.why: to promise God's blessing on a faithful home and to tie it to the welfare of Jerusalem and Israel
settings.readers: Families in the small post-exilic community heard that their homes, fields and children were part of Zion's blessing.
views: Pilgrims blessed before going home (Allen, Kraus).
Used as a blessing for a new household (Goldingay).

title: Plowed, but Not Beaten
sum: Psalm 129 is Psalm 128 in the Greek and Latin numbering. Israel speaks as one person: "Over and over they have attacked me since I was young ... yet they have not won out over me." Enemies plowed long furrows on its back, but the LORD, who is in the right, cut the ropes. The second half prays that all who hate Zion will be like grass on a roof, which withers before harvest and never hears the reaper's blessing.
The psalm joins thanksgiving for survival with a mild curse on Zion's enemies. Its farm images (plowing, harnessing, reaping, binding sheaves) run all the way through.
readings: Read as national thanksgiving
Israel remembers its whole history of oppression, from Egypt onward, and thanks God that it has survived. The call "let Israel say it" (as in 124:1) makes the people speak together.
Read as a prayer of the persecuted
The psalm has been prayed by Jews in every later persecution and by Christians who heard in it the scourged Christ and the suffering church (Augustine).

views.H: The title names no author. Jewish readers link the "youth" of Israel to Egypt (Hosea 11:1).
views.C: Scholars date it after the exile. It is a communal song of confidence: 129:1–4 look back, 129:5–8 pray. The withheld harvest greeting (129:8) is a curse by silence rather than by violence.
views.L: The Liturgy of the Hours uses it at Daytime Prayer. It is less often sung in churches than its neighbors.
views.J: The Midrash on Psalms compares Israel to a borrowed heifer plowed by ten sons until the owner breaks the yoke and cuts the ropes.
views.X: Augustine read the speaker as the whole church, persecuted from Abel onward, and the plowmen as the persecutors whose cruelty only deepened the furrows for a harvest. Many Christians hear Christ's scourging in 129:3 (Isaiah 50:6; Matthew 27:26).

deep.b:
The curse in 129:5–8 is woven from farm life. Grass on a flat roof of packed earth sprouts after rain but has no depth, and it dries up "before it can be pulled" (129:6). It never fills a reaper's hand or the fold of a binder's robe (129:7). And no one passing will give the harvest greeting, "The LORD's blessing on you!" (129:8), which reapers exchanged as in Ruth 2:4. The enemies of Zion are pictured not as destroyed in battle but as a crop that comes to nothing.

Compared with Psalm 137, the curse is mild: it asks for failure and shame, not death. But it shows the same conviction found in all the curse psalms: those who attack the people and city God chose stand against God himself, and their work cannot last. See the topic on the curse psalms.

echoes: Psalm 124:1; Hosea 11:1; Isaiah 51:23; Isaiah 50:6; Micah 3:12; Ruth 2:4; 2 Kings 19:26; Isaiah 37:27; Matthew 27:26; 2 Corinthians 4:8–9

settings.what: Israel's thanks for survival and a curse on Zion's haters
settings.by: Israel speaking as one person, led by a voice that calls "let Israel say it"
settings.to: the congregation (129:1–4), then about Zion's enemies (129:5–8)
settings.when: no event is named; scholars think of the whole story of oppression up to and after the exile
settings.why: to remember that Israel has survived every attack by God's justice, and to ask that hostility to Zion come to nothing
settings.readers: Jews after the exile, and in every later persecution, sang it as the confession of a people that would not be destroyed.
views: A communal song of confidence (Allen, Hossfeld and Zenger).
Prayed in every age of persecution, with no one setting (Goldingay, Midrash Tehillim).

title: From the Depths
sum: Psalm 130 is Psalm 129 in the Greek and Latin numbering, known in the West by its Latin first words, De profundis. From the depths a speaker calls on the LORD and confesses that if God kept a record of guilt, no one could stand. "Yet forgiveness is found with you." He waits for the LORD more than night watchmen wait for the morning, then turns to all Israel: wait for the LORD, for loyal love and full redemption are with him, and he will redeem Israel "from all its guilty deeds."

It is the sixth of the church's seven Penitential Psalms, a psalm of the Catholic Office of the Dead, and the psalm Martin Luther set as the hymn "Aus tiefer Not schrei ich zu dir" (1524). Jews pray it in the Ten Days of Repentance.
readings: Read as a prayer of the guilty

The "depths" are the depths of sin. The speaker does not plead innocence but casts himself on God's forgiveness, and finds in it a reason to fear and wait for God. This is the reading of the Penitential Psalms tradition.
Read as a prayer in deep trouble

The "depths" are deep waters of distress (69:2; Jonah 2:2–3), and the speaker's guilt is only part of it. He waits for rescue as watchmen wait for dawn, and calls all Israel to wait for redemption from exile and sin alike.

views.H: The title names no author. The Targum heads it, like the other Songs of Ascents, "a song said on the ascents from the abyss" (see the chapter page of Psalm 120).
views.C: Scholars call it an individual lament turned into a song of trust for the community (130:7–8). The language of forgiveness (selichah, 130:4) is late and rare, and many date it after the exile. The alternation of YHWH and Adonai is carefully built.
views.L: The Roman Liturgy of the Hours sings Psalm 130 at Night Prayer on Wednesdays, at Evening Prayer on Christmas and other feasts, and in the Office of the Dead; it was long said at every Catholic funeral and for the souls in purgatory. In the Orthodox Church it is one of the "Lord, I call" psalms sung at every Vespers, with hymns of the day set between its verses. Luther's hymn is sung in Lutheran churches, and Bach built his cantata BWV 38 on it (1724). Jews say it in the Ten Days of Repentance and in times of trouble.
views.J: Rashi reads 130:4 as meaning that God gave no agent the power to forgive (Exodus 23:21), so that people would fear God alone. The Targum reads the watchmen of 130:6 as those who wait to offer the morning sacrifice. The Talmud learns from 130:1 that one should pray from a low place (Bavli Berakhot 10b).
views.X: Augustine read the psalm as the cry of the whole Christ, head and body, from the depths of mortal life. Luther called 32, 51, 130 and 143 the "Pauline Psalms," because they teach forgiveness by grace and not by works. John Owen's Practical Exposition upon Psalm 130 (1668) became a classic of Puritan devotion, and John Wesley heard the anthem "Out of the deep" at St Paul's on the afternoon of 24 May 1738, the day his heart was "strangely warmed."

deep.b:
The psalm moves from the depths to the dawn. Verses 1–2 cry for a hearing; 3–4 confess that guilt would crush everyone, "yet forgiveness is found with you"; 5–6 wait; 7–8 turn outward to Israel. The verb "wait" (qavah) and "hope" (yachal) are repeated, and "the watchmen for the morning" is said twice: the long night drags on, but morning is sure. In the temple, the morning sacrifice could begin only when a lookout reported the eastern sky light "as far as Hebron" (Mishnah Tamid 3:2), and the Targum reads the watchmen in that way.

The final line widens the hope: God "will redeem Israel / from all its guilty deeds." Redemption (padah) was the word for buying free a slave or a firstborn. Here what Israel needs to be freed from is its own guilt. Christians heard this fulfilled in Jesus, who "will save his people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21, fresh rendering).

From the 500s (Cassiodorus) the Western church grouped seven Penitential Psalms: 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143. They were said on the Fridays of Lent and before confession, and Psalm 130 was said in the Office of the Dead, at burials, and for the souls in purgatory; in many Catholic countries church bells rang at dusk for the De profundis. Protestants kept the psalm but read it as a confession of forgiveness by grace. Luther's hymn "Aus tiefer Not" (1523–24), one of the first Lutheran hymns, puts 130:3–4 in these terms: before God "no one can boast," and grace alone forgives. Settings by Josquin, Lassus, Bach, Mozart, Schoenberg and many others show how deep the psalm runs in Western music.

echoes: Psalm 69:1–2; Psalm 32:1–5; Psalm 143:2; Psalm 51:1–4; Jonah 2:2–3; Lamentations 3:55–58; Exodus 34:6–7; Isaiah 21:11–12; Matthew 1:21; Romans 3:20–24; Titus 2:14; 1 John 1:9

settings.what: A cry from the depths that becomes a call to all Israel to hope
settings.by: one person in deep trouble and aware of guilt, who then speaks to Israel (130:7–8)
settings.to: the LORD (130:1–4), the speaker's own soul and the listeners (130:5–6), and Israel (130:7–8)
settings.when: no event is named; many scholars place it after the exile, perhaps used by pilgrims at the temple
settings.why: to confess that no one can stand before God except by his forgiveness, and to lead the whole people to wait for his redemption
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, aware that the exile was judgment for sin (Lamentations 1:5), prayed it as a confession and a hope for full redemption.
views: A personal prayer later used by the community (Allen, Kraus).
A confession of sin in worship (the church's tradition).
Spoken at the temple by a pilgrim (Crow).

traditions.q: What does "forgiveness is found with you" teach about how sinners are made right with God?
views: A "Pauline Psalm" (Luther, with 32, 51 and 143): no one can stand on their own works (130:3), and God forgives by grace alone, received by faith. Luther's hymn "Aus tiefer Not" puts this into song.

Forgiveness is God's free pardon, grounded in Christ's atonement, and it produces reverent fear and assurance (130:4); John Owen's Exposition upon Psalm 130 (1668) applies it to the troubled conscience.

One of the seven Penitential Psalms: the sinner confesses guilt and receives forgiveness, which in justification also renews him inwardly (Catechism 1987–1992); the psalm is prayed in the Office of the Dead for souls being purified.
Sung at every Vespers among the "Lord, I call" psalms: forgiveness is God's mercy healing the sinner, received in repentance and the life of the church, rather than a legal verdict.

traditions.q: The De profundis is prayed for the dead. May the living pray for the departed? (The text every view here argues over is 2 Maccabees 12:45, where Judas had atonement made for the dead "to free them from the sin"; 2 Maccabees is held as Scripture by the Catholic and Orthodox churches but not by Protestants or Jews, and its card, "Can sins be cleansed after death, as the Catholic teaching on purgatory holds?", sets out the views.)
views: Yes: the church prays for the dead who are being purified in purgatory (Catechism 958, 1030–1032), and Psalm 130 is a psalm of the Office of the Dead and of funerals.
Yes: the departed are alive in God and the church prays for them in memorial services, though without the Western teaching on purgatory.
Masses and prayers to release souls from purgatory are rejected (Smalcald Articles II.2); Psalm 130 is the prayer of the living sinner who trusts God's forgiveness.
Prayer is not to be made for the dead (Westminster Confession 21.4); the psalm belongs to the living, who wait for the LORD's redemption.

title: Like a Weaned Child
sum: Psalm 131 is Psalm 130 in the Greek and Latin numbering. In three verses, the speaker says his heart is not proud and he has not reached for things too great for him. Instead he has quieted his soul, like a weaned child lying on its mother. Then he calls Israel to wait for the LORD forever.
It is one of the shortest psalms and one of the most intimate. It stands right after the cry from the depths (130), as rest after struggle, and ends with almost the same words as 130:7.
readings: Read as a psalm of humility
The speaker has stopped grasping at what belongs to God and has learned contentment. Like a weaned child, he no longer cries for what he wants but rests near the one he trusts.
Read as a mother's psalm

The image of a child lying on its mother, and "my soul lies on me" (131:2), may be spoken by a woman carrying her child. If so, it is one of the few psalms in a woman's voice, using a mother's experience to speak of trust in God.

views.H: The title says "Of David." Rashi hears David contrasting himself with Solomon, who made "great things": buildings, gardens and pleasures.
views.C: Scholars call it a song of trust. Some suggest a woman speaker. The closing verse addressing Israel may have been added when the psalm entered the collection.
views.L: The Liturgy of the Hours uses it at Evening Prayer on Tuesday of week three. It is prayed in many Christian traditions of silent or contemplative prayer, and is often used in retreats and in prayer for the anxious.
views.J: The Targum turns 131:2 into a picture of study: "I put my hand to my mouth and kept my soul silent until I heard the words of the Torah, like a weaned child at its mother's breasts." Rashi reads the child as one still nursing, close to its mother.
views.X: Christians have linked it to Jesus' call to become like little children (Matthew 18:3–4) and to Mary's song (Luke 1:48–52). Charles Spurgeon called it "one of the shortest Psalms to read, but one of the longest to learn."

deep.b:
Israelite children were nursed for two or three years (1 Samuel 1:22–24; 2 Maccabees 7:27). A nursing infant cries and grasps for milk; a weaned child can lie on its mother simply to be near her, with no demand. The speaker has "leveled" his soul (as a plowed field is leveled, Isaiah 28:25) and "hushed" it. He has given up anxious ambition and reached a quiet trust.

The psalm does not despise great things. It refuses to make them the measure of life, or to strain after "wonders beyond me" that belong to God (Job 42:3). The Greek translators read the oath form differently and made the verse a curse on himself if he had been proud (see the variant), but the Hebrew picture is gentle. Isaiah uses a mother's care for God's own love: "Can a woman forget her nursing child?" (Isaiah 49:15, fresh rendering).

echoes: Psalm 130:7; Psalm 62:1; Isaiah 28:25; Isaiah 30:15; Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 66:12–13; 1 Samuel 1:22–24; Matthew 11:29; Matthew 18:3–4; Philippians 4:11–12

settings.by: one person, perhaps a woman (131:2); the title names David
settings.when: no event is named; it is a personal song of trust later joined to the pilgrims' collection
settings.why: to show humble trust as the right posture before God and to call the whole people to it
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, with little power and much reason to worry, learned from it to wait for the LORD in quiet.
views: A personal song of contentment (Allen, Kraus).
Spoken by a mother with her child (some modern scholars).

title: David's Oath and the LORD's Oath
sum: Psalm 132 is Psalm 131 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It is the longest of the Songs of Ascents and is built on two oaths. First the people ask God to remember David, who swore not to rest until he found a dwelling for the LORD; they tell how the ark was found in the fields of Jaar and brought up, and cry, "Up, LORD, to your place of rest!" (132:1–10). Then God's oath answers: he swore to set David's sons on the throne, he chose Zion as his home forever, and he promises food, salvation, joy, and a horn and lamp for David's anointed (132:11–18).

Verses 8–10 appear, with changes, as the end of Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 6:41–42). The psalm joins the two great choices of God, David and Zion, and became a key text for the hope of a coming son of David.
readings: Read as a festival of the ark
The psalm was sung in a procession that brought the ark up to the temple, re-enacting David's journey (2 Samuel 6). Priests, king and people took part, and the king prayed for God's favor (132:10).
Read as messianic hope

After the exile there was no king. The promise of a "horn" to "spring up" for David (132:17) and the oath that he would always have a son on the throne pointed to a future anointed king. The New Testament hears it fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 2:30; Luke 1:69).

views.H: The title names no author. Chronicles puts 132:8–10 in Solomon's mouth (2 Chronicles 6:41–42), and many Jewish and Christian readers have taken the psalm as Solomon's prayer at the dedication. The historical books tell of David's wish to build (2 Samuel 7:1–2) but not of his oath.
views.C: Most scholars think the psalm comes from the time of the kings, perhaps used at an annual festival of the ark and the dynasty, with a prophetic oracle in 132:11–18 (Kraus, Mowinckel). Others date it after the exile as a hope for David's line. The conditional promise in 132:12 differs from the unconditional one in 2 Samuel 7 and Psalm 89 (see the note on 132:12).
views.L: The Book of Common Prayer (1662) appoints Psalm 132 for Evening Prayer on Christmas Day, with 89 and 110. The Liturgy of the Hours uses it at Evening Prayer. The suffrages of Anglican Morning and Evening Prayer, "Endue thy ministers with righteousness; and make thy chosen people joyful," come from 132:9.
views.J: When the Torah scroll is returned to the ark in the synagogue, the congregation sings 132:8–10, "Arise, LORD, to your resting place ...," just as Numbers 10:35 is said when it is taken out. Rashi and the Targum read 132:10 of Solomon bringing the ark into the temple, and the Talmud tells that the temple gates would not open for the ark until Solomon prayed, "Remember the loyal love shown to David" (Bavli Shabbat 30a). The Targum reads 132:17 as "a glorious king for the house of David."
views.X: Peter's sermon at Pentecost cites 132:11: God swore to David to set one of his descendants on his throne, and David foresaw the resurrection of the Christ (Acts 2:30–31). Catholic liturgy sings 132:6–10, 13–14 at the Vigil Mass of the Assumption, reading "the ark of your strength" of Mary, whom the Litany of Loreto calls "Ark of the Covenant" (Catechism 2676). Zechariah's song ("a horn of salvation ... in the house of David his servant," Luke 1:69, fresh rendering) and the angel's words to Mary (Luke 1:32–33) echo the psalm.

deep.b:
Chronicles ends Solomon's dedication prayer with lines that are almost the same as 132:8–10. The site's Plain of each is set side by side here; where the Hebrew is the same, the English is the same.

Psalm 1322 Chronicles 6

132:8 Up, LORD, to your place of rest, / you and the ark of your strength!6:41 up, LORD God, to your place of rest, / you and the ark of your strength!

and your faithful ones shout for joy.and your faithful ones be glad in good things.
132:10 For the sake of David your servant, / do not turn your anointed one away.6:42 LORD God, do not turn your anointed one away. / Remember the loyal love shown to David your servant.

The differences. (1) Chronicles adds "And now" (ve'attah), joining the lines to the prayer before them. (2) It adds "LORD God" (YHWH Elohim) three times. (3) Psalm 132:8 has limnuchatekha, Chronicles lenuchekha: two forms of "your place of rest," with no difference in meaning. (4) "Righteousness" (tsedeq) in the psalm is "salvation" (teshu'ah) in Chronicles, the word the psalm itself uses in God's answer (132:16). (5) "Shout for joy" (yeranenu) becomes "be glad in good things" (yismechu vattov). (6) Instead of "For the sake of David your servant," Chronicles has "Remember the loyal love shown to David your servant" (chasdei David, "the loyal loves of David"), echoing Isaiah 55:3, and puts it last, so that the prayer ends with David. (7) In Chronicles the Leningrad Codex reads "your anointed ones" (plural); the site's Plain there follows the singular, as in the psalm (see the variant at 2 Chronicles 6:42).

Scholars usually think Chronicles quotes the psalm and adapts it: it brings in the answer of 132:16 ("salvation") and the theme of God's hesed to David, which Chronicles loves (Japhet; Williamson). Others suggest both draw on a common temple liturgy. Either way, the Chronicler made the psalm's prayer part of the story of the first temple's dedication, so that later readers heard Psalm 132 as Solomon's song.

The psalm has two halves of almost equal length. In the first, David swears to the LORD (132:2); in the second, the LORD swears to David (132:11). David seeks a "place" and a "dwelling" (132:5); God declares Zion "my place of rest forever" (132:14). The people pray that the priests be clothed in righteousness and the faithful shout for joy (132:9); God answers that he will clothe them in salvation and they will "shout and shout for joy" (132:16). The prayer "do not turn your anointed one away" (132:10) is answered by "I have set a lamp in order for my anointed one" (132:17).

The two choices of God, of David's house and of Zion, belong together here, as in 78:68–70 and 2 Chronicles 6:5–6. When Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC, both seemed lost (89:38–51; Lamentations 2:6–9). The psalm kept the promise alive.

settings.by: a leader or the people (132:1–10), then a priest or prophet speaking God's words (132:11–18)
settings.to: the LORD (132:1–10), then the king and people, hearing God's oath

Solomon's prayer, as Chronicles presents it (traditional).
A prayer for the restoration of David's line (Hossfeld and Zenger).

traditions.q: Is the ark of Psalm 132:8 a picture of Mary?
views: Yes, as a type: Mary carried the presence of God in Christ, so the church sings Psalm 132 at the Vigil of the Assumption and calls her "Ark of the Covenant" (Catechism 2676).
Yes: hymns of the Theotokos call her the ark of God's holiness, gilded by the Spirit, and the Entry of the Theotokos into the Temple is read in that light.
No: the ark stands for God's presence with his people, fulfilled in Christ himself (John 1:14); Mary is honored as mother of the Lord, not as the ark.
No: the ark was a sign of God's covenant presence, fulfilled in Christ and his church; the psalm's promise concerns David's son.

title: Brothers Together
sum: Psalm 133 is Psalm 132 in the Greek and Latin numbering. In three verses it praises brothers living together as one: it is like the oil poured on Aaron's head that runs down his beard to his robes, like the dew of Hermon falling on the hills of Zion. There the LORD has ordered the blessing, life for all time.
The two pictures both flow down: the oil from the high priest's head, the dew from the high mountain. Unity among God's people is a blessing that comes from above.
readings: Read as the unity of the tribes at the feast
Pilgrims from every tribe gathered at Zion. The psalm celebrates their unity as brothers, and the blessing that God gives there.
Read as family wisdom
"When brothers live together" is the phrase of Deuteronomy 25:5 for brothers who keep their father's land undivided. A family proverb about harmony among heirs became a song about God's people.

views.H: The title says "Of David." Jewish readers have connected it with the reunion of the tribes under David (2 Samuel 5:1–3).
views.C: Scholars call it a wisdom saying with priestly imagery, perhaps from after the exile, when unity between returning exiles and those who had stayed was hard (Ezra 4; Nehemiah 5). Some think verse 3 originally described the northern dew of Hermon and the southern hills of Zion together, as a picture of north and south united.
views.L: Augustine said this psalm "gave birth to monasteries," because brothers who heard it longed to live together as one. It is sung at ordinations, in ecumenical services, and at the meetings of many church bodies. The Hebrew song "Hinneh mah tov" is sung around the world.
views.J: The Targum reads the brothers as "Zion and Jerusalem, like two brothers." Rashi reads it of the time when God will dwell in the temple with Israel, who are called his brothers and friends. It is often sung at the Sabbath table.
views.X: Christians have read the oil as the Holy Spirit poured on Christ, the head, flowing down to his body the church (Acts 2:33; 1 John 2:20, 27), and the psalm as a picture of the early church that was "one heart and soul" (Acts 4:32, fresh rendering). Hilary of Poitiers and Augustine both wrote on it this way.

deep.b:
Both images of 133:2–3 use the verb yarad, "come down," three times. The holy oil of Exodus 30:22–33, mixed with myrrh and spices, was poured on Aaron's head at his ordination (Leviticus 8:12); it was not dabbed but poured so freely that it ran down his beard to "the neck of his robes," the opening of the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:32). The blessing poured on the priest who bore the names of all the tribes (Exodus 28:21) reached the whole of him.

Hermon, about 2,800 m (9,200 ft) high, is the source of the Jordan and famous for heavy dew. Its dew cannot literally fall on Zion, about 200 km (125 miles) south. The picture is of the north's richest blessing falling on Jerusalem. In a dry land, dew in summer is life (Hosea 14:5; Genesis 27:28). The psalm ends: "There is where the LORD has ordered the blessing: / life for all time."

echoes: Genesis 13:8; Deuteronomy 25:5; 2 Samuel 5:1–3; Exodus 29:7; Exodus 30:22–33; Leviticus 8:12; Hosea 14:5; John 17:21–23; Acts 2:44–47; Acts 4:32; Ephesians 4:3; 1 John 2:20

settings.by: a teacher or pilgrim; the title names David
settings.when: no event is named; scholars think of pilgrims gathered at Zion for a feast, or of a family proverb applied to Israel
settings.why: to praise the unity of God's people and to say that God's blessing rests where they live as one
settings.readers: The small community after the exile, divided by old quarrels and new hardships, heard it as a call to live as brothers around Zion.
views: The tribes gathered at Zion (Allen, Kraus).
Hermon and Zion as Israel and Judah united (some scholars).

title: Bless the LORD by Night
sum: Psalm 134 is Psalm 133 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It is the last of the Songs of Ascents. Someone calls on the LORD's servants who stand in his house through the night to lift their hands and bless the LORD, and the answer comes back: "May the LORD bless you from Zion, / maker of heaven and earth."
In three verses it closes the collection that began far from home (120). The pilgrims, about to leave, bless the night watch in the temple; the priests bless them in return.
readings: Read as the pilgrims' farewell
At the end of the feast, the departing pilgrims call on the priests and Levites keeping the night watch to go on blessing God, and receive a last blessing for the road.
Read as night worship
The servants are the Levite singers, who served "day and night" (1 Chronicles 9:33). The psalm is a call to praise at night, answered by the priestly blessing.

views.H: The title names no author. The Targum heads it, like the others, as a song said on the ascents from the deep.
views.C: Scholars see a short liturgy of exchange: 134:1–2 a call, 134:3 a blessing. Night watches in the temple are known from 1 Chronicles 9:27, 33 and from the Mishnah (Middot 1:1).
views.L: From Benedict's Rule onward Psalm 134 has been sung at Compline, the church's last prayer before sleep, in the Western church (Rule of Benedict 18); the Roman Liturgy of the Hours keeps it at Night Prayer on Saturday evening.
views.J: A saying of Rabbi Yochanan applies "who stand in the LORD's house night after night" to scholars who study Torah at night: Scripture counts it as if they served in the temple (Bavli Menachot 110a). Psalm 134 is said with the other Songs of Ascents on winter Sabbath afternoons.
views.X: Christians have read the servants as all who pray at night (Luke 2:37; Acts 16:25) and the blessing from Zion as the blessing of Christ on his church. The psalm's place at Compline made it, for centuries of monks and nuns, the last psalm of the day.

deep.b: The fifteen Songs of Ascents end where they were going. Psalm 120 began "next to one who hates peace"; 121 set out with eyes on the hills; 122 stood in the gates; 123–131 passed through contempt, danger, tears, toil and forgiveness; 132 brought the ark to its rest; 133 gathered the brothers; and 134 stands in the house of the LORD at night. The last line gathers the collection's key words: "bless," "from Zion," and "maker of heaven and earth" (121:2; 124:8). The pilgrims who received help "from the LORD" now receive his blessing "from Zion."

echoes: 1 Chronicles 9:27; 1 Chronicles 9:33; Numbers 6:24–26; Psalm 128:5; Psalm 121:2; Psalm 124:8; Psalm 135:1–2; Luke 2:37; Acts 16:25; 1 Timothy 2:8

settings.what: A call to bless the LORD and a blessing in answer
settings.by: departing pilgrims or a leader (134:1–2), then a priest (134:3)
settings.to: the LORD's servants in the temple (134:1–2), then a worshiper ("you," 134:3)
settings.when: the title: a Song of Ascents; scholars suggest the last night of a feast, as pilgrims prepare to go home
settings.why: to close the pilgrimage with praise of God and his blessing on those who came
settings.readers: Jews after the exile, returning from the feasts to towns far from Jerusalem, carried the blessing from Zion home.
views: The pilgrims' last exchange with the night watch (Allen, Crow).
A call to the Levites' night praise (Kraus).

title: Chosen as His Treasure
sum: Psalm 135 is Psalm 134 in the Greek and Latin numbering. It opens and closes with "Praise the LORD!" and calls the LORD's servants in the temple courts to praise him, because he is good and because he chose Jacob as his own private treasure. It praises him as Lord of nature, who does whatever he wants in heaven, earth and sea, and as Lord of history, who struck Egypt's firstborn and the kings of Canaan and gave Israel their land. The nations' idols are silver and gold that cannot speak or hear. Then all Israel, the priests, the Levites and all who fear the LORD are called to bless him.
Almost every line echoes another passage of Scripture (see the note on 135:1). Psalm 135 is a twin of Psalm 136: both tell creation, exodus, and the gift of the land, and both name Sihon and Og.
readings: Read as temple praise after the exile
The psalm gathers familiar words into a hymn for the temple courts. Its four groups of worshipers (135:19–20) reflect the second temple, with priests and Levites as separate orders.
Read as a confession against idols
At its center (135:15–18) is the mockery of idols from Psalm 115. Israel's God acts; the gods of the nations cannot. Choosing Israel, he also proves himself above every god (135:5).

views.H: The psalm has no title, only "Praise the LORD!" at both ends. It continues the call of 134:1 to the "servants of the LORD" who stand in his house.
views.C: Most scholars date it after the exile, as an anthology of older texts: Deuteronomy, Exodus, Jeremiah 10 and Psalm 115. Some think it was composed to pair with Psalm 136 in festival worship.
views.L: In the Orthodox Church, Psalms 135 and 136 (134 and 135 in the Greek) are the polyeleos, "much mercy," sung at Matins on feasts with lamps lit and "Alleluia" after each verse. The Liturgy of the Hours uses Psalm 135 at Evening Prayer.
views.J: Psalm 135 is said in the Sabbath and festival morning service before Psalm 136. In the Talmud, one opinion counts the Great Hallel from 135:4, "For Yah chose Jacob," to the end of 136 (Bavli Pesachim 118a). Rashi reads "you who fear the LORD" (135:20) as converts.
views.X: Christians read the choice of Israel as God's "own private treasure" (135:4) in the light of 1 Peter 2:9, where the church is "a people for God's own possession" (fresh rendering), and the mockery of idols in the light of Paul's "we know that an idol is nothing" (1 Corinthians 8:4, fresh rendering).

deep.b:
The two psalms follow the same outline. Both call on worshipers to praise (135:1–3; 136:1–3), both praise God as Creator (135:6–7; 136:4–9), both tell the plague on the firstborn (135:8; 136:10), the defeat of "powerful" or "great kings," Sihon and Og (135:10–11; 136:17–20), and the gift of the land "as an inheritance" (135:12; 136:21–22). Psalm 135:12 and 136:21–22 are almost word for word the same.

The difference is in form. Psalm 135 is a hymn in free verse that ends with a call to bless the LORD; Psalm 136 adds a refrain to every line. Psalm 135 has the mockery of idols; Psalm 136 has the sea crossing and the wilderness. Together they set the praise of the one God who creates, chooses and saves at the close of the pilgrim songs.

echoes: Exodus 19:5–6; Exodus 18:11; Exodus 3:15; Deuteronomy 7:6; Deuteronomy 32:36; Jeremiah 10:3–16; Psalm 113:1; Psalm 115:3–11; Psalm 134:1; Psalm 136:17–22; 1 Peter 2:9; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6

settings.what: A hymn of praise for God's choice, power and deeds
settings.to: the LORD's servants in the temple (135:1–3, 19–21), the LORD himself (135:13), and Egypt (135:9)
settings.when: no title; scholars place it in the second temple's worship, perhaps at a festival
settings.why: to praise the God who chose Israel and acts in nature and history, and to set him against powerless idols
settings.readers: Israel after the exile, a small people in a world of great empires and their gods, confessed that its God alone does what he wants.
views: A hymn for festival worship (Allen, Kraus).
A learned mosaic of older texts (Hossfeld and Zenger).

title: His Loyal Love Is Forever
sum: Psalm 136 is Psalm 135 in the Greek and Latin numbering. In 26 verses it gives thanks to the LORD, the God of gods and the Lord of lords, and every verse ends with the same refrain: "for his loyal love is forever." It tells of creation (the heavens, the earth on the waters, the sun, moon and stars), the exodus (Egypt's firstborn, the Sea of Reeds cut in pieces, the wilderness), the defeat of Sihon and Og, the gift of the land, and a later rescue "when we were brought low." It ends with the God who gives food to every living thing.
The Talmud calls it the Great Hallel (Bavli Pesachim 118a). Its refrain is Israel's oldest response in worship, sung at the ark's arrival, the temple's dedication, and the second temple's foundation.
readings: Read as a litany of history
Every act of God, from creation to the gift of the land to the present rescue, is an act of hesed. History is the story of his loyal love, told verse by verse.
Read as a responsive song
A leader sang the first line of each verse and the people or choir answered with the refrain, as 2 Chronicles 7:3, 6 and Ezra 3:11 describe. The psalm is a script for worship.

views.H: The psalm has no title. Chronicles sets the refrain in David's and Solomon's worship (1 Chronicles 16:34, 41; 2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3, 6), and Ezra in the laying of the second temple's foundation (Ezra 3:11).
views.C: Scholars date the full psalm after the exile; the title "God of the heavens" (136:26) is typical of the Persian period (Ezra 1:2; Nehemiah 1:4). The refrain is older. The Great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPs-a) has an extra refrain at 136:8 and lacks "great" in 136:4, and the fragment 4QPs-n reads "Israel his people" in 136:22 (see the variant on 136:8).
views.L: Jews recite Psalm 136 in the morning service of Sabbaths and festivals, and many say it at the Passover seder after the Hallel. In the Orthodox Church it is half of the polyeleos sung at festal Matins. The Liturgy of the Hours uses it at Evening Prayer, and Anglican chant books often set it with the refrain sung by all. John Milton paraphrased it at fifteen ("Let us with a gladsome mind," 1623), still a common hymn.
views.J: The Talmud explains the name Great Hallel: God "sits in the heights of the world and gives food to every creature," and the 26 refrains match the 26 generations from creation to the giving of the Torah, when the world lived by God's hesed alone (Bavli Pesachim 118a; Rashi on 136:26). Rashi reads the Sea of Reeds cut "into pieces" as twelve paths, one for each tribe.
views.X: Christians have sung Psalm 136 as praise for the whole history of salvation, continued in Christ. The refrain is echoed in many Christian hymns and in the responsive "for his mercy endures forever" of Anglican and Lutheran liturgy.

deep.b:
The refrain ki le'olam chasdo, "for his loyal love is forever," comes in all 26 verses. Hesed is the love that keeps covenant faith: steady, generous, more than duty requires (Exodus 34:6–7). Older English Bibles render it "mercy" (KJV), newer ones "steadfast love" or "faithful love"; the site uses "loyal love" everywhere. The refrain makes a claim about every line: creation is hesed, the plague on Egypt is hesed, the defeat of Sihon is hesed, and daily bread is hesed.

The psalm moves in an order much like Genesis to Joshua: God of gods and Lord of lords (136:1–3); creation of heaven, earth and lights (136:4–9; Genesis 1); the exodus (136:10–15; Exodus 12–15); the wilderness (136:16); the conquest east of the Jordan (136:17–20; Numbers 21); the land (136:21–22; Joshua). Then it steps into the present: "who remembered us when we were brought low" (136:23), perhaps the exile and return. The last line returns to all creation: "who gives food to every living thing" (136:25).

Jewish tradition knows three groups of praise psalms. The "Egyptian Hallel" is Psalms 113–118, sung at the feasts. The "daily Hallel" is Psalms 145–150, said every morning. The "Great Hallel" (Hallel haggadol) is Psalm 136. The Talmud records three opinions on where the Great Hallel begins: Psalm 136 alone; or from "For Yah chose Jacob" (135:4); or from the last Song of Ascents (134) (Bavli Pesachim 118a). Rabbi Yochanan explains why it is "great": God "sits in the heights of the world and distributes food to every creature," as 136:25 says.

Rabbi Tarfon held that the Great Hallel is said over a fifth cup at the Passover seder (Bavli Pesachim 118a), and many families recite Psalm 136 at the end of the seder to this day. The Mishnah also says that when rain came after a fast for drought, the people said the Great Hallel (Mishnah Taanit 3:9).

settings.by: a leader or choir (the first half of each verse) and the congregation (the refrain)
settings.to: the congregation, calling them to give thanks to the LORD
settings.when: no title; Chronicles and Ezra place the refrain at great moments of temple worship; scholars date the full psalm after the exile
