The "us" of 136:23–24 is the returned exiles (Hossfeld and Zenger).

title: By the Rivers of Babylon
sum: Psalm 137 is Psalm 136 in the Greek and Latin numbering. Beside the rivers of Babylon, the exiles sit and weep as they remember Zion. They hang up their lyres on the poplars, because their captors demand a song of Zion and they cannot sing the LORD's song on foreign soil. The speaker swears never to forget Jerusalem: let my right hand forget, let my tongue stick to my palate. Then the psalm turns to the enemies. "Remember, LORD, against the people of Edom / the day of Jerusalem," when they cried, "Tear it bare!" And to Babylon: "Happy is the one who pays you back ... Happy is the one who grabs your babies / and shatters them on the rock."

It is the most quoted song of exile in the world and one of the hardest psalms in the Bible. The beauty of its first six verses and the violence of its last three belong to the same grief. The curse is treated below and on the topic page on the curse psalms.
readings: Read as the cry of victims

The speaker has seen Jerusalem's children killed (Lamentations 2:20–21; 4:10) and asks God to repay Babylon in kind. The psalm does not take vengeance; it hands it to God and to God's justice. It keeps the victims' pain in Scripture instead of silencing it (Zenger, Brueggemann).
Read as prophecy or allegory

Calvin heard the Spirit announcing Babylon's fall, as Isaiah 13:16 and Jeremiah 51 did. Augustine and Benedict read "Babylon's babies" as sinful thoughts in their infancy, to be dashed against Christ, the rock, before they grow.

views.H: The psalm has no title in the Hebrew. Codex Sinaiticus has the title "Of David"; the Gallican Latin has "Of David, of Jeremiah" (David Hieremiae), linking it to Jeremiah, the prophet of the fall of Jerusalem.
views.C: Most scholars date it soon after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, or after the first return; the word "there" (137:1, 3) may look back on Babylon from Jerusalem. The Al-Yahudu tablets (about 572–477 BC) show Judeans settled near Nippur on the canals. The curse matches the law of like for like and the prophets' oracles against Edom and Babylon (Obadiah; Jeremiah 50–51).
views.L: The Roman Liturgy of the Hours uses 137:1–6 at Evening Prayer and leaves out 137:7–9 (General Instruction 131). The Orthodox Church sings the whole psalm at Matins on the three Sundays before Lent, with the polyeleos. The Book of Common Prayer (1662) appoints it whole for the 28th evening. Verdi's chorus "Va, pensiero" in Nabucco (1842), the reggae song "Rivers of Babylon" (the Melodians, 1970; Boney M, 1978) and Don McLean's round have made its opening known worldwide.
views.J: Jews say Psalm 137 before the grace after meals on weekdays, and Psalm 126 on Sabbaths and feasts. Many grooms recite 137:5–6 before breaking a glass at the wedding, and the Talmud reads "the best of my joys" as the ashes put on a bridegroom's head in memory of Jerusalem (Bavli Bava Batra 60b). The Targum gives 137:7 to Michael, the angelic prince of Jerusalem, and 137:8 to Gabriel, the prince of Zion. In later Jewish reading Edom stands for Rome, which destroyed the second temple.
views.X: Augustine preached that every Christian lives "by the rivers of Babylon," a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem in exile in this world. Frederick Douglass quoted 137:1–6 in his Fourth of July speech of 1852 to speak for the enslaved. On how Christians pray or omit the last verses, see the box below.

deep.b:
The psalm's last three verses ask God to remember Edom's cry on the day of Jerusalem (137:7), and bless whoever repays Babylon and dashes its babies on the rock (137:8–9). Readers should not soften what the words say. Killing the children of a conquered city was a known horror of ancient war (2 Kings 8:12; Hosea 13:16; Nahum 3:10), and the prophets foretold it for Babylon itself (Isaiah 13:16). The speaker asks that Babylon suffer what Jerusalem suffered: the law of like for like (Exodus 21:23–25; Jeremiah 50:15, 29).

Several points help to read it honestly. It is a prayer, not an act. The speaker does not take revenge but gives it to God, "Remember, LORD" (137:7; compare Romans 12:19). It comes from victims. These are exiles who have seen their city burned and their children killed (Lamentations 2:19–21; 4:10). It is about justice. The prayer is that the empire that destroyed others be destroyed, as the prophets said it would be (Jeremiah 51:24, 56). It is not the last word. Jesus taught, "keep loving your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44), and prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). Yet the martyrs in Revelation still cry, "how long until you judge the people who live on the earth and pay them back for our blood?" (Revelation 6:10), and Revelation repeats the psalm's demand against the last Babylon: "Pay her back as she has paid others" (Revelation 18:6).

Jewish practice keeps the whole psalm in prayer: on weekdays it is said before the grace after meals, verses 7–9 included. The Targum puts 137:7 in the mouth of Michael, prince of Jerusalem, and 137:8 in the mouth of Gabriel, prince of Zion, so that the cry becomes a plea made in heaven, and later Jewish readers heard it as God's coming judgment on Edom, the name they gave to Rome. Christian traditions have answered differently. Some keep the whole psalm in prayer as an honest cry left with God; some read the last verse as prophecy; some as allegory; some leave the verses out of public worship. The card below sets out the main Christian positions. See the topic on the curse psalms for 35, 69 and 109.

deep.h: Edom on the day of Jerusalem
deep.b: Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea, was Judah's neighbor and "brother" (Genesis 25:23–26; Deuteronomy 23:7). When Babylon took Jerusalem, Edomites joined in the looting and cut off fugitives (Obadiah 10–14; Ezekiel 25:12–14; 35:5–15; Lamentations 4:21–22); 1 Esdras 4:45 says they burned the temple. Edom then moved into southern Judah, later called Idumea. The prophets announced its judgment (Jeremiah 49:7–22; Malachi 1:2–4). After the Romans destroyed the second temple in AD 70, rabbinic writers used "Edom" as a name for Rome, and Psalm 137:7 became a prayer against every empire that destroys Jerusalem.

echoes: Ezekiel 1:1–3; Ezekiel 3:15; Jeremiah 29:4–7; Jeremiah 50:15; Jeremiah 50:29; Jeremiah 51:24; Jeremiah 51:56; Isaiah 13:16; Isaiah 47:1–3; Lamentations 4:21–22; Obadiah 10–14; Daniel 6:10; Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:19; Revelation 6:10; Revelation 18:6; Revelation 18:21

settings.what: A lament of the exiles, an oath of memory, and a curse on Edom and Babylon
settings.by: an exile, or a singer who had been in exile, speaking for the community ("we") and then as "I" (137:5–6)
settings.to: the community (137:1–4), Jerusalem (137:5–6), the LORD (137:7), and Babylon (137:8–9)
settings.when: no title in the Hebrew; scholars date it to the Babylonian exile (after 587 or 586 BC) or soon after the first return
settings.why: to keep the memory of Jerusalem alive in exile, to refuse to make its songs entertainment for captors, and to put the injustice done to Zion before God
settings.readers: Jews after the exile and in every later diaspora sang it as their oath not to forget Jerusalem, and wrestled with its curse.
views: Looking back on Babylon from Jerusalem ("there") (Allen, Hossfeld and Zenger).
The Gallican title links it to Jeremiah (Latin tradition).

traditions.q: Should Christians pray Psalm 137:9, and if so, how?
views: The Liturgy of the Hours omits 137:7–9, as it omits Psalms 58, 83 and 109 and other curse verses, because of "psychological difficulty" for Christian prayer (General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours 131). Augustine and Benedict's Rule read the babies as evil thoughts dashed against Christ the rock (Rule of Benedict, Prologue 28).

The whole psalm is sung at festal Matins on the three Sundays before Lent, as Christians begin the journey of repentance from "Babylon"; the fathers read the babies as the first stirrings of sin, to be destroyed before they grow.

Calvin read 137:9 as the Spirit's announcement of God's just judgment on Babylon, echoing Isaiah 13:16, not as private revenge. Churches that sing only psalms sing the whole psalm, as in the Scottish Psalter of 1650.

Bonhoeffer taught that the curse psalms are prayed through Christ, who bore God's vengeance on sin at the cross; Christians pray them by handing vengeance to God and praying for the enemy's conversion.

The 1662 Prayer Book appoints the whole psalm; C. S. Lewis called the last verses "devilish" yet held they show what cruelty does to its victims, and that we should not pretend otherwise. The Episcopal Church's 1979 Prayer Book lectionary appoints 137:1–6 with verses 7–9 in parentheses, as optional.
